cover.alt: The household works to clear the home field after the ash fall; Ásta uses her wooden bowl.
cover.art_brief: Ink and watercolour, established visual bible. April 1875 after the Askja ash at Hamrar in Jökuldalur: grey home field and turf house, Bjarni, Siggi and Óli with wooden shovels, Guðrún and Helga clearing a thin line of grass near the house, Ásta with her wooden askur. Pumice heaps at the ravine edge where Óli throws it. Greyish-brown light porous pumice, grey to black ash. Fully clothed period woollen farm clothing. Gamla-Manga by the doorway watching rather than shovelling. No visible volcano, lava or modern objects. No lettering.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Tún er grasið hjá bænum. Um sumarið er heyið þar.
Um páskana féll askan á túnið, og vikurinn var á túninu.
Dag eftir dag mokaði fólkið á Hömrum, og Ásta mokaði með aski.
Þegar kvöldið kom, var gras hjá bænum aftur.
words_with_history.note_en: Tún is the home field: the manured, walled hayfield round an Icelandic farmhouse. It is the same word as English town (Old English tūn, 'enclosure, farmstead'), Dutch tuin 'garden' and German Zaun 'fence': first a fence, then the land it enclosed, and in English at last a whole town.

pronunciation_note.rule: In baula and Baulaðu, au is the diphthong [øy]: start with a rounded vowel like the vowel in French peu or German schön and glide towards a rounded ee sound. Keep it distinct from á. The cow’s call in the refrain repeats this au.

grammar.note_en:
The past tense places an event or state before the moment of speaking: “was”, “had”, “shovelled”. The present describes what is true now: “is”, “has”, “shovels”. From this chapter, the narrator tells the story in the past. People still use the present when speaking about now. Askan féll. Nú fellur hún ekki. (s025) means “The ash fell. Now it is not falling.” Ásta hears the difference: the falling is over. Í gær var vikur á túninu, og í dag er vikur á túninu! (s048) means “Yesterday there was pumice on the home field, and today there is pumice on the home field!” Both tenses can occur in one speech turn. A time word helps establish the situation; it does not mechanically change a verb.

Vera, “to be”, has var with a singular third-person subject, varst with þú, and voru with a plural third-person subject. Ásta var (s003) is “Ásta was”; Varst þú þar, Manga? (s061), “Were you there, Manga?”; Hendur Sigga voru rauðar og heitar (s050), “Siggi’s hands were red and hot”. The hands can be referred to as þær, “they”, but the table quotes the actual noun subject. No ég var, við vorum or þið voruð cell is supplied: those combinations are absent from this chapter’s story. Hafa, “to have”, has hafði for one person and höfðu for more than one in the occurrences here. Siggi hafði litla skóflu (s032) means “Siggi had a small shovel”; Þau höfðu son og eina kú, Búkollu (s096), “They had a son and one cow, Búkolla”. These past shapes need learning as shapes, rather than adding -aði to er or hefur.

For the productive weak class taught here, remove the infinitive’s final -a to get the stem, then add -aði in the third-person singular: kalla → kall- + -aði → kallaði, “call → called”; moka → mok- + -aði → mokaði, “shovel → shovelled”. Compare the familiar present hann kallar, “he calls”, with hann kallaði, “he called”; hann er, “he is”, with hann var, “he was”. These are explanations of known present forms, not new story-table cells. Mokar (s035, s045) is “shovels”; mokaði (s031), “shovelled”, for one person; mokuðu (s030), “shovelled”, for several. The plural has -uðu; stem a changes to ö before this u, a sound change called u-umlaut. Thus jarma → jarmaði → jörmuðu (s133) means “bleat → bleated (one) → bleated (several)”. With byrja the plural is byrjuðu (s047), “began (several)”, beside byrjaði (s010), “began (one)”. Read each form as encountered; do not invent an unattested plural to complete a grid.

The other table entries mean: skoðaði, “looked at”; kastaði, “threw”; hreinsaði / hreinsuðu, “cleared or cleaned”, with one / several subjects; leitaði / leituðu, “searched”, with one / several subjects; baulaði, “mooed”; opnaði, “opened”; fóðraði, “fed (animals)”. The dash means that this chapter has no corresponding story form, not that the verb lacks that form. The table is for looking up the chapter’s evidence, not for reciting a whole paradigm.

Recognise these irregular items as words for now; they are not a paradigm or production exercise: fer → fór, “goes → went”; kemur → kom, “comes → came”; sér → sá, “sees → saw”; fellur → féll, “falls → fell”; segir → sagði, “says → said”; spyr → spurði, “asks → asked”. Their plural items here are fóru, “went”, komu, “came”, féllu, “fell”, and sögðu, “said”. Weak classes beyond -aði are taught in Kafli 12, and strong past patterns in Kafli 13. Baulaðu nú, Búkolla mín! (s101) means “Moo now, my Búkolla!” Learn that call as a supported formula; do not derive or practise its command form here.

Einu sinni var dimmt á Hömrum (s014) means “Once upon a time it was dark at Hamrar”. It opens a tale. Manga’s plain Einu sinni (s059) means “Once”, one time in the past; it does not turn her mother’s account into a fairy tale. Þegar introduces a clause locating one event in relation to another: Þegar kvöldið kom, var gras hjá bænum aftur (s037), “When evening came, there was grass by the farmhouse again”. The whole when-clause occupies the first position; the main clause’s finite verb var comes next, before its subject gras. Compare Þegar kindurnar komu út, leituðu þær að grasi (s131), “When the ewes came out, they searched for grass”: after the opening clause, leituðu precedes þær. The past time belongs to the events, not to þegar itself. Use this when-pattern with the past forms already met here; the full word-order system comes later.
